title: Strings
subtitle: Runes and Ribbons
martuIntro:
Text in quotes is a [[string]]: letters strung together like beads, in order. Each letter has a position, counted from 0, the same as the items in a list.
In this unit you take text apart and build it again. You cut out a piece, put quote marks inside quotes, and use tools like `.upper()` that hand back a changed copy.
You have seen all of this in the campaign: `.lower().capitalize()` tidying the dialogue options, `"█" * caster["mana"]` in the mana bars, and `+ str(...)` gluing numbers into words. Back then it was somebody else's code. This time it is yours.
goals: Read one letter of a word by its position, cut out a piece with a [[slice]], and count the letters
Explain why one letter of a word can't be changed, and build a new word instead
Put quote marks and new lines inside text
Use text tools (methods) that hand back a new copy, like all capitals, and keep the copy
Cut a sentence into a list of words, glue a list back into one line, and turn the text `"48"` into the number 48
Fill names and numbers into the blanks of a line, like Mad Libs, in two ways: with an f-string, and with the campaign's `+` and `str()`
Build a status bar for any numbers, like the campaign's mana bars

questions.explain: The stamp `"#" * 3` is `"#" + "#" + "#"`, so it makes `###`. Then `str(n)` turns the number 3 into text, so `+` can glue it on: `### 3`.
Python uses PEMDAS, like math class: `*` goes before `+`. 3 * 4 is 12, then 2 + 12 is 14.

exercises.title: Letters have positions
exercises.martu:
Text is letters in a row, like the items in a list. Each letter has a position, counted from 0, the way a ruler starts at 0. `[0]` is the first letter, and `[-1]` is the last:
```text
 T  e  l  e  g  u  n
 0  1  2  3  4  5  6
-7 -6 -5 -4 -3 -2 -1
```
`len()` counts the letters: `Telegun` has 7.
A [[slice]] copies a piece, like quoting a few words of a poem in English class. `[0:4]` takes positions 0, 1, 2 and 3. The end is left out, the same as with lists. You know this from the chalk wall, my wall of gap numbers (the hours between bursts), yes?

anotherWay.label: Letters on tiles
anotherWay.text:
Picture each letter on a numbered tile, like the gaps on the chalk wall:
```text
M o o n   S t e p
0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8
```
`[0:4]` takes tiles 0, 1, 2 and 3: `Moon`. The space on tile 4 is left out. The end tile is never taken.

anotherWay.label: One step at a time
anotherWay.text:
1. For the sign, count to the comma, starting at 0.
2. Use that position as the end of the slice. The end is left out, so the comma is too.
3. In the loop, `name[0]` is this pass's first letter. Glue it on the end of `initials`.

anotherWay.label: From English class
anotherWay.text: *Seven* is how many, and *seventh* is which one. `Telegun` has seven letters, and its seventh letter, n, is at position 6. A position counts from 0, so it is always one less.
Mar'tu numbers the chalk wall from 0: gap 0, gap 1, gap 2. A word is a wall of letters. Same counting, same square brackets.

exercises.title: Letters can't change
exercises.martu:
You can't change one letter of a string. Programmers call this [[immutable]]: it can't change. Think of a word printed in a book: you can't swap one letter on the page, but you can print a new page. So `word[0] = "G"` stops Python with an error. Build a new string instead, like `spell = "N" + spell[1:]`.
`spell[1:]` is the rest of the word, from position 1 to the end. Glue a new first letter onto it, then put the new string in the variable with `=`. A new `=` always replaces what a variable holds. A list lets you swap one item. Text does not.
Lucky's canteen (his water bottle) has a label that says `Plug`. It should say `Glug`.

anotherWay.label: A painted sign
anotherWay.text: A word is like a sign painted on a board. You can't peel off one letter. You paint a new board, copy the letters you want, and hang it where the old one was.

1. `word[1:]` copies `lug`, the rest of the word.
2. `"G" + ...` glues a G in front: `Glug`.
3. `word = ...` puts the new string in the variable. The old `Plug` is gone.

anotherWay.label: Why can't text change?
anotherWay.text: Python keeps each string sealed, so it never changes behind your back. Every change you see is a new string put in the variable. That is why tools like `.lower()` hand back a copy. You meet them in the next lesson, Words That Change Shape.

exercises.title: Escape marks
exercises.martu:
Quote marks start and end text. So how do you put a quote mark *inside* text without ending it? Put an [[escape mark]] in front of it: a backslash, `\`. `\"` means *this quote mark is part of the text*. So `print("Bo: \"Run.\"")` shows `Bo: "Run."`. `\n` is an escape mark too: it starts a new line, like pressing Enter.
In English class, a quote inside a quote uses single marks. I want real double marks, so you need the backslash.
The backslash itself never shows: Python reads it as a signal, not a letter.
If you like, after the steps (it's not a step): take one backslash out, press Run, and read the box in the Console.

anotherWay.label: Where the text ends
anotherWay.text:
```text
"Mar'tu: "NOT a ...
^        ^
start     Python thinks
          the text ends
```
A backslash in front, `\"`, tells Python: this is not the end, only a quote mark.
In a story, a speaker's words sit inside quote marks. A backslash is like whispering to Python: "this one is part of the story, keep reading".

1. Write the outer quotes: `print("")`.
2. Type the words inside.
3. Wherever a `"` belongs inside, type `\"`.
4. Wherever a new line belongs, type `\n`.

exercises.title: Bars one more time
exercises.martu:
A bar is a tape diagram, like in math class: the full part plus the empty part make the whole. Make one for Lucky's canteen of glug (his drink), for any numbers, like this one:
```text
Glug [▓▓░] 2/3
```
In `make_bar(current, maximum)`, `current` is the sips left and `maximum` is how many sips the canteen holds.
Stamp one `▓` for each sip left and one `░` for each sip gone: `"▓" * 2` is `"▓" + "▓"`. Then glue on the numbers with `+`, made into text with `str()`. You know all three from the campaign's mana bars, `"█" * caster["mana"]`. Now they work together.

anotherWay.label: The bar in pieces
anotherWay.text:
```text
Glug [ ▓▓  ░  ]  2 / 3
      |   |      | |
      |   |      | maximum
      |   |      current
      |   empty * (3 - 2)
      full * 2
```

1. `used = maximum - current`: the sips gone.
2. Stamp `full` `current` times, and `empty` `used` times: the blocks.
3. Glue `"Glug ["` on the front, then `"] "`, `str(current)`, `"/"` and `str(maximum)` on the end.
4. `return` the whole bar.
The campaign's mana bar is the same build: `filled = "█" * caster["mana"]`, then the empty blocks, then `str(...)` for the numbers. Your glug bar is that bar, built by you.

anotherWay.text: `*` goes before `-`. Parentheses go before both, like PEMDAS.

1. Work out the days gone: week minus days left.
2. Stamp `░` that many times.
3. Glue it on.

checkpoints.text: Fix line 6 so the bar holds `week` blocks in all: `▓` for each day left, `░` for the rest.
hints: Read the title of the box in the Console. Then read Python's last line: `unsupported operand type(s) for -: 'str' and 'int'`. Python stopped at line 6.
Python uses PEMDAS, so it does `*` before `-`. That makes `"░" * week` text first. Then it tries to take a number away from text.
Parentheses go first, like PEMDAS in math class: `"#" * (5 - 2)` stamps 3 marks.
Write `bar = bar + "░" * (week - days_left)` on line 6.

items.title: Words That Change Shape
items.summary: Text tools (methods) that hand back a changed copy: capitals, chains, split and join, strip, replace and find. Then f-strings, and two functions of your own.

exercises.title: Methods hand back a copy
exercises.martu:
A [[method]] is a tool you use with a dot. The dot asks the text to do a job, the way you speak to someone by name: `line.upper()` means *line, give me a copy in capitals*. You get a new copy, and the text in `line` does not change. Catch the copy with `=`, or it is gone: `name = name.title()`.
[[.upper()]] hands back a copy in CAPITALS. [[.title()]] hands back A Capital On Each Word, like a book title. `.lower()` and `.capitalize()`, from earlier units, work the same way.
Lucky asks the same thing about everything: "What's in it for me?" A string answers every job the same way: with a new string.

anotherWay.label: Catch the copy
anotherWay.text: A method is like asking Gearshift for a copy of a map. He hands you a new map. If you don't take it, it falls on the floor. Your old map is still the old map. `line = line.upper()` takes the copy and keeps it.

1. `line.upper()` makes `"SHIELD UP."` and hands it back.
2. `line = ...` puts that copy in `line`.
3. `print(line)` shows what `line` holds now.
Module 1 wrote `dialogue_input = dialogue_input.lower()`. Same shape: the method on the right, the same name on the left to catch the copy.

checkpoints.text: Change line 2 so `line` keeps the capital copy. You should see `SHIELD UP.` in the Console.

exercises.title: Chain two methods
exercises.martu:
A [[chain]] is one method right after another, like `said.lower().capitalize()`. Python reads it left to right. `.lower()` hands back a new string, and `.capitalize()` works on that copy. In math class, it is like two function machines in a row: what comes out of the first goes into the second.
You have done this in two steps before. In the campaign's Module 1, my line went through two tidy steps:
```python
said = said.lower()
said = said.capitalize()
```
A chain does both on one line:
```python
said = said.lower().capitalize()
```

anotherWay.label: One copy at a time
anotherWay.text:
```text
"WHAT IS THE DECAY?"
   .lower()
"what is the decay?"
   .capitalize()
"What is the decay?"
```
Each step down is a new copy. `return` hands back the last one.

1. `raw.lower()` hands back a copy in small letters.
2. `.capitalize()` works on that copy and hands back a new one with a capital first letter.
3. `return` hands that last copy back.

anotherWay.label: A shortcut with .capitalize()
anotherWay.text: `.capitalize()` already makes the rest small, so `raw.capitalize()` alone gives the same here. The campaign chains both to be sure.

exercises.title: Split and join
exercises.martu:
[[.split()]] cuts text into a [[list]] of pieces, like cutting a sentence strip into word cards in English class. Empty parentheses cut at every space: `"Moon Step".split()` gives `['Moon', 'Step']`. `.split(". ")` cuts at each period and space instead. To glue a list back into one text, ask the glue: `" ".join(words)`. The text before [[.join()]] goes between the pieces, like the commas in a list of items.
What comes back from `.split()` is a list, not text: count it with `len()`, read it by position. Python shows each piece with `'` marks. It is the same text.
Bomb Shell talks in short, clipped sentences: "Latch stuck. Shield up."

anotherWay.label: Cut, then glue
anotherWay.text:
```text
"Latch stuck. Shield up."
   .split(". ")
['Latch stuck', 'Shield up.']

["Barrier's", "holding."]
   " ".join(...)
"Barrier's holding."
```
`.split` is scissors: you say where to cut. `.join` is glue: you hold up the glue and say what to stick together. You never ask the paper to glue itself.

1. `report.split(". ")`: a list of sentences.
2. `len(report.split())`: split at spaces, then count.
3. `int(hours_text) + 1`: text to number, then math.
4. `" ".join(words)`: the glue first, then the list.

anotherWay.label: Why the glue does the joining
anotherWay.text: The glue is the one piece of text that goes between each two items. So you ask the glue to do the joining, and hand it the list: `" ".join(words)`. The list only hands over its items.

exercises.title: Clean-up tools
exercises.martu:
Three more [[method|methods]], like the tools in a word processor. [[.strip()]] cuts the spaces off both ends, like trimming the edges of a page. [[.replace()]] swaps old words for new ones, like Find and Replace: `.replace(old, new)`. [[.find()]] hands back the position where some text starts, like Find (Ctrl+F), or `-1` when it isn't there.
Here `-1` means *not found*. It is not the last letter. All three match capitals exactly. And like every string method, they hand back something new, so catch it: `tag = tag.strip()`.
Lucky left a note on the mantel (the shelf over the fireplace). It has spaces at both ends, and it is wrong.

anotherWay.label: Three tools
anotherWay.text:
```text
"  It's a compass.  "
  .strip()
"It's a compass."
  .replace(...)
"It's a Ley Clock."
  .find("Ley")
7
```
Strip is trimming the ragged edges off a page. Replace is crossing out a word and writing a new one. Find is running your finger along the line until you reach the word, and counting the steps.

1. `note = note.strip()`.
2. `note = note.replace(old, new)`, old words first.
3. `note.find("Ley")` counts from 0. Not there? -1.

exercises.title: f-strings
exercises.martu:
An [[f-string]] is text with blanks, like Mad Libs in English class. Put an `f` right before the quotes, and write each variable inside curly braces `{ }`. Python fills each blank with what the variable holds. When `name` holds Lucky and `mana` holds 26, `f"{name}: {mana} mana"` gives `Lucky: 26 mana`. Inside `{ }`, no `str()` is needed.
The campaign builds the same line another way, gluing with `+` and `str()`:
```python
name + ": " + str(mana) + " mana"
```
Read both. Write whichever you like. If you want, put your own hero in `name`: any name in quotes.

anotherWay.label: The same line, twice
anotherWay.text:
```text
name + ": " + str(mana)
  |      |       |
  v      v       v
f"{name}: {mana}"
```
Each glued piece moves inside one pair of quotes.

1. Write `f"` and the closing `"`.
2. Copy the text pieces in, in order.
3. Where a variable was glued in, write its name inside `{ }`. Drop every `+` and `str()`.

anotherWay.label: Why read both?
anotherWay.text: The campaign's `cast_spell` says `caster["character_name"] + " doesn't have enough mana to cast " + spell_name + "."`. Read it like a sentence: text, a value, text, a value. An f-string says the same thing in one pair of quotes.

exercises.title: Two functions of your own
exercises.martu:
Now write two functions of your own, built from tools you know. A function is a recipe with a name, as in Unit 3: the same steps, for any line you hand it. Lucky answers every request the same way. Bomb Shell answers in three words, then stops.
1. `lucky_reply(request)` hands back the request, stripped and capitalized, then ` What's in it for me?`.
2. `clip(sentence)` hands back the first three words of `sentence`, joined with spaces, then a period.
You know every piece already: `.strip()`, `.capitalize()`, `.split()`, a slice and `.join()`. In the last lines, ask Lucky anything you like.

anotherWay.label: Copy after copy
anotherWay.text:
```text
"  carry this  "
  .strip()
"carry this"
  .capitalize()
"Carry this"
  + ask
"Carry this What's ..."
```

`clip`:
1. `sentence.split()`: a list of words.
2. `[:3]`: the first three, or fewer.
3. `" ".join(...)`: back to text.
4. `+ "."`: Bomb Shell's period.
Lucky never says yes without asking his question. Bomb Shell never says a fourth word. Each function is one hero's habit, written once and used for any line.

items.title: Quiz: Words That Change Shape
items.summary: 8 questions on text tools, split and join, find, f-strings and a function. Retake it as often as you like.

questions.explain: Left to right: `.lower()` makes every letter small, then `.capitalize()` makes the first one big. The line keeps the copy, so it prints `What is the decay?`.
`" ".join(...)` glues the list into one text with a space between. `.split(",")` cuts at the comma and hands back a list, so `print` shows its square brackets and quotes.
There is no Z in EXIT, so `.find` hands back -1: not found. It is not the last position, which is 3.

questions.q: This should print `Latch stuck.`, but it stops with an error. Fix it.
questions.explain: A list has no `.join`. Ask the glue instead: `" ".join(words)` puts a space between the words.

questions.q: Which line prints the same as the last line of this code?

whyWrong.1: With no `f`, the braces print as they are: `{name}: {mana}`.
whyWrong.2: Text plus a number is an error: `mana` needs `str()` before `+` can glue it.
whyWrong.3: In quotes, `name` is only the letters n, a, m, e. No quotes means look inside the variable.

questions.explain: Both give `Lucky: 26`. The f-string fills the blanks `{name}` and `{mana}`. The `+` line glues the same pieces, with `str()` for the number.
`.strip()` cuts the spaces off both ends, and `.replace("X", "D")` swaps the X. Each copy is caught in `sign`, so the square brackets show `EDIT` with no spaces.

questions.q: Fill the blank so this prints `Bomb Shell`.
questions.explain: `.title()` gives every word a capital, like a book title. `.capitalize()` would give `Bomb shell`.

questions.q: This should print `SHIELD UP.`, but it prints `None`. Fix it.
questions.explain: No `return`, so `shout` hands back `None`, Python's word for nothing. End it with `return line`.

items.title: Extra practice: Letter by Letter
items.summary: Extra practice, 3 exercises. Ask if a report says red, count the blocks in a bar with a loop, and fix Lucky's name tag.

exercises.title: Is red in the report?
exercises.martu:
[[in]] works on text too. `"red" in report` asks: are the letters r, e, d, in that order, somewhere inside `report`? Python answers `True` or `False`. In Unit 4, `in` asked if a value was in a list. On text, it looks for letters, like Find (Ctrl+F) on a web page.
`in` matches letter for letter, and capitals count: `"red" in "RED"` is `False`. Ask a lower-case copy instead. `.lower()` is a [[method]], a tool you use with a dot: `report.lower()` means *report, give me a copy in small letters*. Then capitals stop mattering.
The Ley Clock counts down to the next burst, a blast from the leylines. It goes yellow before one, and once went red. Does Gearshift's report say red?

anotherWay.label: Sliding a window
anotherWay.text:
```text
report: i t   w e n t   r e d
look:               [r e d]
```
`in` slides `red` along the report, one letter at a time. If all three letters match somewhere, the answer is `True`.

anotherWay.label: Searching a page
anotherWay.text: Find on a web page (Ctrl+F) works like `in`. With *Match case* turned on, Find says `RED` and `red` are different. So you make everything small letters first, with `.lower()`, then search.

`"red" in report.lower()` with `report = "It went RED."`:
1. `report.lower()` makes a copy: `"it went red."`.
2. `in` looks for `red` in the copy, and finds it.
3. The answer, `True`, goes back with `return`.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: In the campaign, `dialogue_input = dialogue_input.lower()` made Mar'tu's line all small letters. It's the same method here: it makes the copy before `in` asks its question.

exercises.title: Count the full blocks, letter by letter
exercises.martu:
Text is letters in a row, so a [[for loop]] can walk it. In Unit 6, `for gap in chalk_wall:` handed you one gap each pass. `for letter in bar:` hands you one letter each pass, like spelling a word out loud: `T`, `o`, `r`.
A mana bar (a hero's magic power, drawn as blocks) is text too: a `█` for each point of mana, and a `░` for each point used. In the campaign, you made a bar from a number. Here you go the other way: count the `█` letters to get the number back, like counting tally marks in math class.
I test your function with bars it has never seen, so count with the loop. A typed-in number never changes.

anotherWay.label: One letter each pass
anotherWay.text:
```text
bar:     █  █  █  ░  ░
pass:    1  2  3  4  5
block?   ✓  ✓  ✓  .  .
blocks:  1  2  3  3  3
```
Five passes, one per letter. Only a `█` adds 1.

anotherWay.label: Counting coins
anotherWay.text: Pour coins out of a jar and slide them past one by one. Each time you see a gold one, say the next number. The loop is the sliding. The `if` is the question *is this one gold?*

1. `blocks = 0` before the loop.
2. `for letter in bar:` takes the next letter.
3. `if letter == "█":` asks about it.
4. If yes, `blocks = blocks + 1`.
5. After the last letter, `return blocks`, lined up with `for`.
Walk with `for`, ask with `if`, add with `blocks = blocks + 1`, hand back after the loop.

With other names: `for mark in shout:` then `bangs = bangs + 1`, indented, adds 1 for every mark.
Write `for letter in bar:` in place of the note (the comment), then `blocks = blocks + 1` indented under it.

exercises.title: Broken spell: three bugs in a name tag
exercises.martu:
You can't change one letter of a string, the same as a word on a printed page. In Unit 4, `chalk_wall[2] = 47` changed one item of a list, but `word[0] = "C"` stops Python with an error. Build a new string and put it back in the variable: `word = "C" + word[1:]`.
Lucky's name tag says `Pucky`. Gearshift's spell to fix it has three loud bugs: mistakes that stop Python. Each time, read the box in the Console. Its title says what went wrong, Python's last line says it in Python's words, and the line number says where. Fix that line, press Run, and see what comes next.

anotherWay.label: Which bug first?
anotherWay.text:
1. Press Run. Python stops at line 2: position 5 is past the end.
2. Fix it and press Run again. A new error is good news: Python got further.
3. Line 4 can't swap a letter. Build a new string.
4. Line 7 measures a number. Measure `bar`.

items.title: Quiz: Rows of Letters
items.summary: Quiz, 6 questions: positions, slices, `len()`, `in`, and why you can't change one letter of a string.

questions.q: This sign hangs on the greenroom door. What will this code print?
questions.explain: `[:9]` starts at position 0 and stops *before* position 9, the comma, like an open dot on a number line. That gives the 9 letters of `Greenroom`.

questions.q: Fill the blank so the program prints `Interior`.
questions.explain: `I` sits at position 11: count the comma and the space too. Leave the end empty, and the slice runs to the end. `[-8:]` works as well: the last 8 letters.

questions.q: Which one reads the last letter of `word`, for a word of any length?

whyWrong.0: Positions stop at `len(word) - 1`, so `word[len(word)]` is one past the end: an IndexError.
whyWrong.2: `word[1]` is the second letter. Positions start at 0.
whyWrong.3: `word[0]` is the first letter, not the last.

questions.explain: `[-1]` counts from the end, so it is the last letter of a word of any length.

questions.q: This code should print `Telegun`, with a capital T. Fix it.
questions.explain: You can't change one letter of a string, so `word[0] = "T"` stops with a TypeError. Build a new string, a T and then everything from position 1 on, and put it back in `word`.
`in` matches letter for letter, and `G` is not `g`, so the first line is `False`. The lower-case copy, `"glow"`, does hold it, so the second line is `True`.
`len()` counts every letter, space and mark, and the space counts as one: 4 + 1 + 5 = 10. The function hands that back, and `print` shows it.

items.title: The Water-Stained Log
items.summary: Project, 7 tasks. Lucky copied the chalk wall in the rain. Split his messy copy, clean it, and turn it into numbers.
items.intro:
Lucky copied Mar'tu's chalk wall, the wall of gap numbers (the hours between bursts), onto paper, in the rain. This is what he handed over. It's on line 3 of your code:
`" 48 hrs| 48 hrs |47 hrs|46hrs | 44 hrs|41 hrs | 37hrs "`
The numbers are in there, buried under bars `|`, spaces and `hrs`. Your job: get clean numbers out. Lucky: "You're welcome."
Seven tasks, in order, under Your tasks. Each one names the note in your code where it goes: `# 1.`, `# 2.`, `# 3.`, `# 4.`, `# 5.`, `# 6.` and `# 7.`.
Before this: the lesson Words That Change Shape (`.split()`, `.strip()`, `.replace()`, `.join()` and [[f-string|f-strings]]), and Biggest and smallest in More List Tools (`sum()`). A loop that adds works too.
items.martu:
Your job: turn messy text into numbers. `.split("|")` cuts the log at every bar `|` and hands back a [[list]] of marks, like cutting a sentence strip into cards. Then clean each mark. `.replace("hrs", "")` swaps every `hrs` for nothing, like Find and Replace. `.strip()` cuts the spaces off both ends. Last, `int("48")` turns clean digits into the number 48.
Each method hands back a new copy, so keep it in a variable, like `word = word.strip()`. `int()` refuses messy text like `"48 hrs"`, so clean first.
I test your code with other messy logs, so build everything from `log`. Don't type in a number you can see.

anotherWay.label: One mark, step by step
anotherWay.text:
```text
" 48 hrs"  -> replace -> " 48 "
" 48 "     -> strip   -> "48"
"48"       -> int     -> 48
```
Every mark takes the same three steps. The loop does them for each one.

anotherWay.label: Washing carrots
anotherWay.text: A muddy carrot: rinse off the mud, cut off the ends, then cook it. A mark: take out `hrs`, strip the ends, then `int()` it. Same order every time, one carrot at a time.

1. `.split("|")`: one messy log becomes a list of messy marks.
2. The loop: replace, then strip, then append the clean text.
3. A loop: `int()` each clean mark, and append the number.
4. `sum()` for the total, then a loop from position 1 for the shrinks.
5. `", ".join(...)` the clean text back into one line.
6. An f-string with `{len(hours)}` and `{total}`.

anotherWay.text: In the campaign, `dialogue_input = dialogue_input.lower()` kept the new copy in the same variable. `clean = clean.strip()` is the same move: a method hands back a new copy, and you keep it.

items.title: The Institute Cipher
items.summary: Project, 5 tasks: build a secret code that moves every letter along the alphabet, then decode Mar'tu's note.
items.intro:
A [[cipher]] is a secret code. Mar'tu still writes notes in the Institute's old cipher, ley shift: every letter moves the same number of steps along the alphabet. That number is the key, and his key is the hour on the Ley Clock, the clock that counts down to the next burst. A note was pinned over the fireplace this morning. The clock said 5.
Five tasks, in order, under Your tasks. In your code, a note (`# 1.` to `# 5.`) marks where each task goes. It all runs here, in the browser.
Before this: the Clock Math article in Unit 1 (`%`, the [[remainder]]), and the lesson Words That Change Shape (`.find()`).
items.martu:
Each letter has a position in `alphabet`, counted from 0: `a` is 0, `b` is 1, `z` is 25. `alphabet.find(letter)` hands you that position, like Find (Ctrl+F) in *Clean-up tools*. For anything not in the alphabet, like a space or a comma, it hands back -1, which means *not found*. Careful: here -1 does not mean the last letter, the way `[-1]` does.
Add `key` to the position. Past `z`, wrap back to `a` with `% 26`, the clock math from Unit 1: 3 hours after 11 o'clock is 2, because a clock wraps at 12. The alphabet wraps at 26.
Then read the letter at the new position. You can't change one letter of a string, so `encode` builds a new string, one letter at a time.

anotherWay.label: The alphabet on a ring
anotherWay.text:
```text
 a  b  c ...  x  y  z
 0  1  2 ... 23 24 25

y + 3: 24 + 3 = 27
27 % 26 = 1  ->  b
```
Past `z`, the count goes around to the start again, like a clock hand past 12.

anotherWay.label: A clock with 26 hours
anotherWay.text: Picture a clock with a letter on every hour, 26 of them. A key of 3 turns the hand 3 hours on. From `y`, three hours on is `b`. `% 26` is the hand going around.

`shift_letter("y", 3)`:
1. `alphabet.find("y")` is 24. It is not -1, so keep going.
2. `24 + 3` is 27, past the end.
3. `27 % 26` is 1.
4. `alphabet[1]` is `"b"`. Hand it back.
Find the position with `.find()`, and leave the letter as it is if that's -1. The new position is `(place + key) % 26`. Build the text letter by letter.

3. Otherwise, hand back the letter at `(place + key) % 26`.

items.title: Name Tags, From Blank
items.summary: Challenge: write `name_tag` from a blank page, with `.upper()` for the capitals and an f-string for the tag.
items.martu:
Write a function from a blank page: `name_tag(name, hours)` hands back a tag like `LUCKY: 48 hrs`. `.upper()` makes the capitals: `"glow".upper()` is `"GLOW"`. An [[f-string]] is text with blanks, like Mad Libs: `f"{item} costs {cost}"` puts each value into its blank, with no `+` and no `str()`.
Then, below the function, print two tags.
I test your function with other names and hours. So build the tag from `name` and `hours`, and don't type it in.
Before this: the lesson Words That Change Shape.

anotherWay.label: One tag, piece by piece
anotherWay.text:
```text
name_tag("Lucky", 48)

caps = "LUCKY"
hours = 48

f"{caps}: {hours} hrs"
 -> "LUCKY: 48 hrs"
```
Each `{...}` is a blank that the value fills, like Mad Libs. Everything else in the quotes stays as you typed it.

1. The `def` line: `name_tag`, then `name` and `hours`.
2. `caps = name.upper()` keeps the capitals copy.
3. One f-string: `{caps}`, a colon and a space, `{hours}`, then ` hrs`.
4. `return` hands the tag back.
5. Below, lined up with `def`: two `print(name_tag(...))` lines.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: The mana bars glued their line with `+` and `str()`. An f-string does the same job in one piece: `f"{caps}: {hours} hrs"` is `caps + ": " + str(hours) + " hrs"`, with no `str()` to forget.

With other names: `def label(item, cost):`, then `return f"{item.upper()} - {cost} gold"`. `label("rope", 5)` hands back `ROPE - 5 gold`.
Write `def name_tag(name, hours):`. Under it, indented: `caps = name.upper()`, then `return f"{caps}: {hours} hrs"`.

exercises.title: Tidy the line
exercises.martu:
Lucky shouts his notes, with extra spaces on both ends. Finish `hush_line(raw)` so it hands back `raw` tidy: no spaces on its ends, small letters, and a capital first letter. A method hands back a new copy. A [[chain]] runs methods left to right, like two function machines in a row in math class: `cry.strip().upper()` cuts the spaces, then makes capitals. Or take a few steps, and keep each copy with `=`. I also test your function with other lines I make up.
Stuck? Skip this task, or go back to *Chain two methods* and *Clean-up tools* in the lesson Words That Change Shape. Tasks you pass here stay ✓ done.

anotherWay.label: One copy at a time
anotherWay.text:
```text
"  SHIELD UP.  "
   .strip()
"SHIELD UP."
   .lower()
"shield up."
   .capitalize()
"Shield up."
```
Each step down is a new copy. `return` hands back the last one.

A method hands you a new copy, and the text in `raw` stays as it was. Keep each copy with `=`, or put the next method right onto it. It's like asking Gearshift for a copy of a map: if you don't take the copy, it falls on the floor.

Bomb Shell keeps his log short: the first three words of every line, and no more. Cut `said` into a list of words, then glue the first three back into one line. [[.split()]] cuts text into a list, like cutting a sentence strip into word cards in English class. A slice keeps the first few cards. Then ask the glue to join them: `"-".join(["moss", "fern"])` gives `moss-fern`. A line with only two words keeps both. I also test your code with other lines I make up, a short one too.
Stuck? Skip this task, or go back to *Split and join* and *Two functions of your own* in the lesson Words That Change Shape. Tasks you pass here stay ✓ done.

anotherWay.label: Cut, keep three, glue
anotherWay.text:
```text
"Pell ran home fast"
   .split()
['Pell', 'ran', 'home', 'fast']
   [:3]
['Pell', 'ran', 'home']
   " ".join(...)
"Pell ran home"
```
`.split` is scissors: it cuts the line into word cards. A slice keeps the first few cards. `.join` is glue: you hold up the glue, a space, and it sticks the cards back into one line.

1. `.split()` on `said` hands back a list of words.
2. A slice, `[:3]`, keeps positions 0, 1 and 2.
3. The glue, `" "`, goes in front of `.join(...)`, and the list goes in its parentheses.

anotherWay.label: The bar in pieces
anotherWay.text:
```text
Fuel 2 of 5 [##...]
     |    |  |  |
     |    |  |  "." * (5 - 2)
     |    |  "#" * 2
     |    tank
     left
```
Each line under the bar points down to the code that makes that piece. `left` and `tank` are the two numbers.

1. Stamp `full` `hp` times. Then stamp `empty` `(top - hp)` times: the parentheses make Python work out the minus first.
2. Put the blocks inside `" ["` and `"]"`.
3. In front go `"Shield "`, `str(hp)`, `" of "` and `str(top)`.
4. Hand back the whole bar with `return`.

questions.explain: Positions start at 0, like a ruler, so `sign[1]` is the second letter, X. A slice stops before its end number, like the open dot on a number line: `[1:3]` takes positions 1 and 2, `XI`. `len()` counts the letters: 4.

questions.answer:
Bomb Shell: 5 days

questions.explain: An f-string is text with blanks, like Mad Libs. Python fills in each `{ }`: `{hero}` is `Bomb Shell`, and `{days - 2}` works out to 5. The `+` line glues the same kind of text: `hero` has no quotes, so Python looks inside the variable, the words in quotes show as they are, and `str(days)` is 7.

questions.q: `word` holds `"Flow"`. Which line, put in place of `# the line goes here`, makes the code print `Glow`?

whyWrong.0: You can't swap one letter of a string, the way you can't swap one letter on a printed page. Python stops: *TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment*.
whyWrong.1: `.replace()` hands back a new copy, and no `=` keeps it, so `word` still holds `Flow`.
whyWrong.3: `word[2:]` starts at position 2, `ow`, so the `l` is lost: `Gow`.

questions.explain: `word[1:]` is everything from position 1 on: `low`. Glue a `G` in front, and put the new string back in `word`. You can't change one letter of a string, like a printed page, so you build a new one.

questions.q:
Which line shows these two lines in the Console?
```text
Lucky: "Mine."
No.
```

whyWrong.0: The quote mark before `Mine.` ends the text early, so Python stops with a SyntaxError. Python's last line guesses you forgot a comma, but that guess is wrong here.
whyWrong.1: `/n` uses the slash `/`, not the backslash `\`. So `/n` is two plain marks: it shows as it is, and everything stays on one line.
whyWrong.2: A comma in `print` shows one space, not a new line: `Lucky: "Mine." No.`, all on one line.

questions.explain: `\"` puts a quote mark inside the text, like quotation marks inside a quotation in English class. `\n` starts a new line, like pressing Enter. The backslashes never show.

choices:
-1
ERROR: IndexError: string index out of range
questions.explain: `.find()` works like Find (Ctrl+F), and capitals count: `"Ash Ward"` has no small-w `ward`. So `.find()` hands back -1, which means not found. But `sign[-1]` is a real position, the last letter, so Python shows `d` with no error. That's a quiet bug: check for -1 before you use it.

['Pell', 'ran', 'home', 'fast']

checkpoints.text: Under `print(ore_gauge(5, 6))`, add a line that prints `Moss: ` and then the bar from `ore_gauge(2, 6)`, in one f-string. You should see `Moss: Ore 2 of 6 [▮▮▯▯▯▯]`.
hints: Look under `print(ore_gauge(5, 6))`, the last line. What goes right before the quotes to make an f-string, and what goes inside its curly braces?

An f-string is text with blanks, like Mad Libs. With other names:
```python
print(f"Oil: {lamp(2, 6)}")
```
The `f` goes right before the quotes. Python calls `lamp` and fills the blank with the text it hands back.
No `+` and no `str()` this time: the f-string fills in the bar for you. Without the `f`, the curly braces print as they are.
Start with `print(f"Moss: {` under `print(ore_gauge(5, 6))`. Then write the call, then `}")`.

items.title: Quick Check 9 · Form B questions
items.summary: Five questions that go with Quick Check 9. To pass the Quick Check, get 4 of the 5 right.

questions.explain: Positions start at 0, like a ruler, so `door[2]` is the third letter, t. A slice stops before its end number, like the open dot on a number line: `[2:5]` takes positions 2, 3 and 4, `ter`. `len()` counts the letters: 8.

An f-string is text with blanks, like Mad Libs. Python fills in each `{ }`: `{name}` is `Lucky`, and `{sips - 1}` works out to 2. The `+` line glues the same kind of text: `name` has no quotes, so Python looks inside the variable, the words in quotes show as they are, and `str(sips)` is 3.

questions.q: `rune` holds `"Glum"`. Which line, put in place of `# the line goes here`, makes the code print `Glug`?

whyWrong.1: You can't swap one letter of a string, the way you can't swap one letter on a printed page. Python stops: *TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment*.
whyWrong.2: `rune[:2]` stops before position 2, so it is only `Gl`: `Glg`.
whyWrong.3: `.replace()` hands back a new copy, and no `=` keeps it, so `rune` still holds `Glum`.

questions.explain: `rune[:3]` is positions 0, 1 and 2: `Glu`. Glue a `g` on the end, and put the new string back in `rune`. You can't change one letter of a string, like a printed page, so you build a new one.

questions.q:
Which line shows these two lines in the Console?
```text
Sign: "EXIT"
Bye.
```

whyWrong.0: A comma in `print` shows one space, not a new line: `Sign: "EXIT" Bye.`, all on one line.
whyWrong.2: The quote mark before `EXIT` ends the text early, so Python stops with a SyntaxError. Python's last line guesses you forgot a comma, but that guess is wrong here.
whyWrong.3: `/n` uses the slash `/`, not the backslash `\`. So `/n` is two plain marks: it shows as it is, and everything stays on one line.

questions.explain: `\"` puts a quote mark inside the text, like quotation marks inside a quotation in English class. `\n` starts a new line, like pressing Enter. The backslashes never show.

But `door[-1]` is a real position, the last letter, so Python shows `p` with no error. That's a quiet bug: check for -1 before you use it.

items.title: Mar'tu's Chalk Notes: Strings
items.summary: Every idea from Unit 9 on one page, with a short example of each. You can print it.

entries.note: Positions start at 0, like a ruler. `[-1]` is the last letter. `len()` counts every letter and space. (Lesson: Strings Are Rows of Letters)
From position 2 up to position 5, but not position 5 itself, like the open dot on a number line. Leave out the start, and it begins at 0.
Like a word on a printed page, a string can't have one letter swapped: `word[0] = "D"` is a TypeError. Build a new string, and put it back in the variable.
`\"` puts a quote mark inside the quotes. `\n` starts a new line, like pressing Enter. The backslash never shows.

entries.concept: Methods hand back a new string
entries.note: A method is a tool you use with a dot, and it hands back a new copy. Alone on a line, the copy is lost. Keep it with `=`: `cry = cry.upper()`. (Lesson: Words That Change Shape)

entries.output:
THE FIRE IS WARM.
The Fire Is Warm.
The fire is warm.
entries.note: `.upper()` makes every letter big, and `.lower()` makes every letter small. `.title()` makes the first letter of each word big, like a book title. `.capitalize()` makes only the first letter big, and the rest small.
Left to right, like two function machines in a row: each method works on the copy the one before it handed back. You've seen this: `option_1.lower().capitalize()`.
Like cutting a sentence strip into word cards. Empty parentheses cut at every space. Text in the parentheses says where to cut. The result is a list: count it with `len()`, and read it by position.
The glue goes first, then `.join`, then the list in parentheses. The glue goes between each two pieces.
`.strip()` cuts the spaces off both ends, like trimming the edges of a page. `.replace(old, new)` swaps every match, like Find and Replace. Capitals must match exactly.
`.find()` works like Find (Ctrl+F). It hands back the position where the text starts, or -1 when the text is not there. Here -1 means *not found*. It is not the last position.
`int` is short for integer, a whole number. Only digits turn into a number. Spaces at the ends are fine, but letters are not.

entries.concept: An f-string, and its `+ str()` twin
entries.note: The same line, two ways. An f-string is text with blanks, like Mad Libs: Python fills each `{ }` with what the variable holds. The campaign uses `+` and `str()`, so learn to read both. (Lesson: Words That Change Shape)
Stamp blocks with `*`. The parentheses make Python work out `most - oil` first, like PEMDAS. You've seen this in the campaign's mana bars. (Lesson: Strings Are Rows of Letters)
`in` asks a yes-or-no question: is this text somewhere inside? Capitals count. To ignore them, ask `report.lower()` instead. (Extra practice: Letter by Letter)
A `for` loop over text takes one letter at a time. (Extra practice: Letter by Letter)
TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment. In plain words: you can't change one letter of text (`str`). Build a new string: `"D" + word[1:]`.

SyntaxError: invalid syntax. Perhaps you forgot a comma? The quote mark before `Fire!` ends the text early. Python's last line guesses a comma, but that guess is wrong here. Put a backslash in front of each quote mark inside: `\"`.
AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'join'. In plain words: a list has no `.join` tool. Ask the glue instead: `" ".join(herbs)`.
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str. In plain words: `+` glues text (`str`) only to text, and `gold` is a whole number (`int`). Use `str(gold)`, or an f-string.
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'twelve'. In plain words: `int()` can't read the word twelve. Only digits turn into a number.

IndexError: string index out of range. In plain words: there is no letter at that position. The last position is `len(rune) - 1`, which is 2. A slice never goes past the end: `rune[:9]` is only `Ash`.
SyntaxError: f-string: expecting '}'. In plain words: a curly brace is missing. Every `{` needs its `}`.
A quiet bug: the code runs, but shows the wrong thing. Without the `f`, the curly braces print as they are. Put an `f` right before the quotes.

entries.concept: No error, wrong answer: -1 read as a position
entries.note: Another quiet bug. `.find()` gave -1, *not found*, but `sign[-1]` reads the last letter, so Python shows `N` with no error. Check for -1 before you use the position.
